**Sources**

### Brown V. Board of Education of Topeka (1954)

*Historical Events · American · [Notion](https://app.notion.com/p/24d44de2a6568035beb7c402cf818e03)*

Unanimous Supreme Court declared that racial segregation in public schools is unconstitutional; separate educational facilities declared to be inherently unequal (reverses 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson ruling that “separate but equal” Jim Crow segregation was legal.

**Sources**

- [Khan Outline](https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/us-history/postwarera/civil-rights-movement/a/brown-v-board-of-education)

<!-- page-notes:24d44de2a6568035beb7c402cf818e03 -->
#### Page notes

<details>
<summary>Historical Context: 1896: Supreme Court decision, Plessy v. Ferguson, declared “separate but equal” Jim Crow segregation legal</summary>

*[Image in Notion](https://app.notion.com/p/24d44de2a6568035beb7c402cf818e03)*

- Resulted in “colored” and “whites only” signs across the South at facilities including water fountains, restrooms, bus stops, movie theaters, swimming pools, and schools
- Eg, in one county, \$149 was spent per year on each white student, but only \$43 on each black student, and black schools didn’t have the same facilities as white schools (eg cafeteria and gymnasium)

</details>

<details>
<summary>The Case</summary>

- Linda Brown (3rd grader), despite living seven blocks from Summer Elementary, had to walk 6 blocks, crossing railroad tracks, to take a bus to Monroe Elementary, due to segregation
- The Topeka, Kansas chapter of NAACP recruited Linda’s father, Oliver Brown, along with a dozen other Black parents, to file suit against the Topeka Board of Education in 1951. By the time it made its way to the supreme court, four other similar lawsuits joined the case
- Linda Brown’s case particularly interesting - Linda’s school was separate but not (measured by funding) unequal - allowed focus on the constitutionality of segregation itself
- Drew on research of two psychologists: Kenneth and Mamie Clark. Argued that the very fact they were sent to different schools damaged their self-esteem, stigmatized them, and adversely shaped their self-image
- Challenged *de jure* segregation of the races
  - de jure: according to the law.
    - Opposite of de facto, which means “according to fact” or “according to reality” to denote instances where what the law dictates is different from what’s actually going on

</details>

<details>
<summary>Thurgood Marshall, the NAACP, and the Supreme Court</summary>

- Thurgood Marshall: the NAACP Chief Marshall
  - Led attorneys to argue the unified case in Brown v. Board before the Supreme Court
  - Later became the first African American Supreme Court Judge
  - ![](https://cdn.kastatic.org/ka-perseus-images/d41d3f10e4343ba7ceffea6de8c0be402cd536b7.jpg)
- NAACP challenged segregation laws for many years prior to Brown; Charles Hamilton Houston (Marshall’s predecessor and mentor) won several smaller lawsuits targeting segregation in education in the 1930s
  - 1950: Marshall won a case before the Supreme Court: Sweatt v. Painter: Court ruled a Texas law school purpoting to offer black students an education equal to that which it offered whites was not - as measured by funding, faculty, or facilities - equal (only 3 basement classrooms for black students and no library)

</details>

<details>
<summary>Brown II</summary>

- Summer 1955: Supreme Court issued implementation ruling
- Ordered that schools undertake desegregation with “all deliberate speed” - meaning not entirely clear
- White citizens in the South organized a “Massive Resistance” campaign against integration
- Note that decision only applied to public schools; did not address Jim Crow laws across the South that applied to restaurants, movie halls, public transportation ,and more
  - Only addressed in 1960s: laws included the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Voting Rights Act of 1965, and the Housing Rights Act of 1968

</details>

### “Massive Resistance” and the Little Rock 9 (1954–1957)

*Historical Events · American · [Notion](https://app.notion.com/p/24d44de2a6568056a23ae394047f9c0b)*

Campaign of “Massive Resistance” emerged in South to oppose desegregation following Brown v. Board. Southern congressmen issued a “Southern Manifesto” denouncing the Court’s ruling, and local resistance slowed and stopped school desegregation. In 1957, President Eisenhower sent federal troops to Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas to enforce the Court’s desegregation order

<!-- page-notes:24d44de2a6568056a23ae394047f9c0b -->
#### Page notes

<details>
<summary>The Southern Manifesto and Massive Resistance</summary>

- Accused the Supreme Court of a “clear abuse of judicial power” and vowed to use “all lawful means to bring about a reversal” of the Court’s decision in Brown.
- 1956: Crowds of angry whites prevented the desegregation of public schools in Texas, Tennessee, and elsewhere
- Since ruling applied only to public schools (not private), some counties closed public schools altogether
- In 1956, Georgia incorporated the Confederate battle flag into its state flag, and South Carolina and Alabama began flying the Confederate battle flag over their state capitol buildings

</details>

<details>
<summary>The Little Rock Nine</summary>

- A small group of African American high school students, accompanied by ministers, were turned away from Central High School in Little Rock by a crowd of white citizens and armed troops from the Arkansas National Guard.
- Elizabeth Eckford: “I walked up to the guard who had let the white students in… When I tried to squeeze past him, he raised his bayonet and then the other guards closed in and they raised their bayonets. They glared at me with a mean look and I was very frightened and didn’t know what to do. I turned around and the crowd came toward me… I tried to see a friendly face somewhere in the crowd - sommeone who maybe would help. I looked into the face of an old woman and it seemed a kind face, but when I looked at her again, she spat on me”
- Governor Faubus only removed the National Guard after a federal district court ordered him to do so. Eisenhower then federalized the Arkansas National Guard and ordered more than a thousand federal troops to Little Rock -
  - First time that federal troops were deployed in a southern state since end of Reconstruction in 1877
  - Eisenhower called attention to the need for law and order, and his obligation as president to ensure carryign out the decisions of the federal courts
  - Eisenhower reminded Americans that segregation was a blight on the international image of the US during the Cold War: “We are portrayed as a violator of those standards of conduct which the peoples of the world united to proclaim in the Charter of the United Nations. There they affirmed ‘faith in fundamental human rights and in the dignity and worth of the human person’ and they did so ‘without distinction as to race, sex, language, or religion’”
- When African American students finally allowed into the school, classrooms were half-empty, and some white students threw down their books and walked out of school
- Once troops were withdrawn following the 1957-1958 school year, Governor Faubus closed Little Rock’s public schools for thee 1958-1959 school year

</details>

### Emmett Till (1955)

*Historical Events · American · [Notion](https://app.notion.com/p/24d44de2a656809f892ac6d1246a1939)*

![Emmett Till](https://cdn.kastatic.org/ka-perseus-images/a2cb9f974b3bfe4afb93aa4b3325fe936fdd4cb5.jpg)

Two white men brutally murdered African American 14-year old Emmett Till for reportedly flirting with a white woman. Till’s mother held an open-casket funeral so the world could see the violence inflicted on her son’s body. His murderers stood trial one month later, and both men were acquitted.

Awakened the rest of the US to the racism that was so prevalent and commonplace in the country

**Sources**

- [Khan Outline on Emmett Till](https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/us-history/postwarera/civil-rights-movement/a/emmett-till)

<!-- page-notes:24d44de2a656809f892ac6d1246a1939 -->
#### Page notes

<details>
<summary>Till’s Murder</summary>

- Till grew up in Chicago and went to Mississippi to visit family, and was unaccustomed to the rigidly maintained racial order in the south
- Carolyn Bryant lied under oath, saying that Till wolf-whistled at her, grabbed her around the waist, and uttered obscenities
  - Bryant has since admitted she fabricated the story and lied under oath
  - Bryant told her husband that Till made sexual advances towards her. Four days later, he and his half-brother kidnapped Till in the middle of the night, beat him, gouged out his eye, then shot and killed him, dumping him in the nearby Tallahatchie River
- When Till’s corpse found, he was recognizable only by the ring he wore; remains were sent to his mother with the coffin nailed shut
- Till’s murder would most likely have gone unnoticed if his mother did not make the brave decision to hold an open casket funeral. Photos were published in the Jet magazine, and over 100,000 attended the funeral.
  - Had the funeral been an official protest, it would have been the largest civil rights demonstration in American history until that point

</details>

<details>
<summary>The Trial</summary>

- Calls for justice throughout the country led to the indictment of Roy Bryant and JW Milam
- Women and African Americans were barred from serving in juries in Mississippi; defendants were tried before an all-male, all-white jury. Till’s great uncle Mose Wright took the stand and identified the men who kidnapped his nephew
- First major media event of the nascent Civil Rights Movement; brought networks and reporters to the small Mississippi town
- Courtroom was segregated, and outside observers were surprised at the sheriff’s conduct, use of racial epithets, and initial refusal to admit black cogressman Charles Diggs into the courtroom
- Defense attorney, in his closing statements, said if the jury convicted Bryant and Milam, “Your ancestors will turn over in their grave, and I’m sure every last Anglo-Saxon one of you has the courage to free these men”. Jury deliberated for 66 minutes before aquitting both men.
  - “We wouldn’t have taken so long if we hadn’t stopped to drink pop” said one of the jurors
- Both men admitted to the killing in a 1956 interview
- The fact that Bryant and Milam were tried for the murder at all was an incredible mark of progress, even though justice wasn’t served. Woke up the rest of the country to the true extent of racism in the US

</details>

### The Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955)

*Historical Events · American · [Notion](https://app.notion.com/p/24d44de2a65680acbaddedcc7c9d5d9f)*

Rosa Parks was arrested for refusing to give up her bus seat so that white passengers could sit in it. Sparked the Montgomery Bus Boycott, during which the Black citizens of Montgomery refused to ride the city’s buses in protest over the bus system’s policy of racial segregation. It was the first mass-action of the modern civil rights era, inspired other civil rights activists across the nation.

The boycott lasted 381 days, ending following a November 1956 ruling by the Supreme Court that segregation on public buses was unconstitutional

Martin Luther King, Jr. emerged as leader of the Boycott.

**Sources**

- [Khan Outline](https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/us-history/postwarera/civil-rights-movement/a/the-montgomery-bus-boycott)

<!-- page-notes:24d44de2a65680acbaddedcc7c9d5d9f -->
#### Page notes

<details>
<summary>Rosa Parks, 42-year old secretary of the Montgomery, Alabama NAACP</summary>

![](https://cdn.kastatic.org/ka-perseus-images/304e0806b8f7a6939c1713e1e3b25a922d7b5b5b.jpg)

</details>

<details>
<summary>Planning of the Movement</summary>

- Rosa Parks selected as the candidate for the public campaign; model citizen and woman of unimpeachable conduct
- After Parks’s arrest, called for a boycott of the city’s buses
- ED Nixon (head of the Alabama NAACP) held meetings with the community in area churches. Produced and distributed leaflets at the curches, reading “don’t ride the bus Monday December 5, and come to a mass meeting at the Baptist Church for further instruction”
- Martin Luther King, Jr (26 at the time) led the boycott, drawing on teachings of Henry David Thoreau and Mahatma Gandhi

</details>

### The March on Washington (1963)

*Historical Events · American · [Notion](https://app.notion.com/p/24f44de2a65680098a1bc9c726e59c1d)*

One of the largest civil rights rallies in US history; famous example of non-violent mass direct action. At the march, Martin Luther King, Jr. delivered his inspirational “I Have a Dream” speech. Highly publicized in the news media and gathered momentum for the Civil Rights Act of 1964

**Sources**

- [Khan Outline on the March](https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/us-history/postwarera/x71a94f19:the-civil-rights-movement-continues/a/the-march-on-washington-for-jobs-and-freedom)
- Video of Martin Luther King, Jr’s I Have a Dream Speech
- Transcript to the I Have a Dream Speech

<!-- page-notes:24f44de2a65680098a1bc9c726e59c1d -->
#### Page notes

- Groups Involved
  - NAACP
  - Student Non-Violent Coordinating Committee (SNCC)
  - American Federation of Labor (AFL-CIO)
  - Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC)
- Opposers of the march
  - Bayard Rustin (though one of the main organizers of the march, concerned it would turn violent and damage the international reputation of the movement)
  - Malcolm X/Black Power Movement: Nonviolent, integrationist approach. Condemned activists for collaborating with whites and accepting donations from whites
- Context
  - 100th anniversary of Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation - major theme of rally was that promises of emancipation remained unfulfilled
  - Began at Washington Monument, ended at Lincoln Memorial
  - Initial idea from A. Philip Randolph - a Black labor leader who headed the Negro American Labor Council at the time of the march, organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters (the first African American Labor union in US History)
  - Purpose
    - Economic justice: Equal access to public facilities and accommodations, housing, education, and jobs
      - Many considered economic deprivation and exploitation of African Americans was just as significant a problem as racism
    - Demand for a federal Fair Employment Practices Act: to ban discriminatory hiring practices
      - Civil Rights Act of 1964, created Equal Employment Opportunity Commission
      - Demand for enforcement of the Fifteenth Amendment: Realized with the passage of the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which eliminated barriers to black enfranchisement erected as part of Jim Crowe
